title: 12 Best Video Production Companies in USA for 2026
summary: The 12 best video production companies in USA, with verified addresses, real cost ranges, and how to tell a production company from a creative agency.
body_markdown:
**Key takeaways:**


- Federal labor data counts 25,298 US motion picture and video production establishments employing about 212,600 people, so the shortlist problem is exclusion rather than discovery.
- California holds 8,194 of them and New York 2,874, but Florida, Texas, Georgia and North Carolina together hold more than 4,300, which means "fly a crew in" is rarely the only option.
- Federal occupational data puts median pay for a producer or director at $83,480 a year, and that single salary buys you none of the camera, lighting, insurance or edit capacity a production company already owns.
- Storyboarding before you shoot is the cheapest schedule insurance there is. It moves the argument to a stage where changes cost nothing.


Video production is the one creative category where the word covers wildly different businesses. A two-person team cutting founder interviews and a company with a soundstage, insurance and a grip truck both describe themselves as a video production company, and both are telling the truth.


The consequence is that shortlists in this category are usually assembled wrong. Search video production companies USA and you get a directory ranking that mixes all of them together, so buyers compare firms that were never competing for the same job, then choose on price. That is how a corporate testimonial ends up costing what a commercial should have.


This list is grouped so you can see which kind of company each one is. We're first on it, and we are clear about the shoots where you should hire a crew with a truck instead.


## Where American video production actually is


It is worth knowing the shape of the industry before shortlisting inside it, because the geography is less concentrated than the Los Angeles and New York reputation suggests.


Bureau of Labor Statistics data counts **25,298 motion picture and video production establishments** operating in the United States, employing roughly 212,600 people, with average annual pay of $122,861.


California dominates with 8,194 establishments and New York follows with 2,874. But the next tier is substantial and frequently overlooked: Florida has 1,476, Texas 1,251, Georgia 940, North Carolina 664, Illinois 626 and Oregon 552.


That distribution matters commercially. Travel and per diems for a crew are real line items, and a competent production company within driving distance of your location often beats a more famous one that has to fly. Georgia and North Carolina in particular built genuine crew depth on the back of film tax incentives, which means the local talent pool is deeper than the reputation implies.


None of this argues against hiring in Los Angeles when the work justifies it. It argues against assuming you have to.


## Production company, creative agency or studio


Three business models compete for the same searches, and the difference determines what you get for your money.


A **production company** owns or reliably books the means of production: crew, camera packages, lighting, sound, and a post pipeline. Brief it well and it will execute beautifully. Brief it vaguely and it will execute your vague brief beautifully.


A **creative agency that produces video** starts earlier, with the message and the strategy, then produces against it. You pay for the thinking, and you should, if the thinking is genuinely undecided.


A **studio facility** rents space, stages and equipment, sometimes with crew attached. If you have your own director and producer, this is the cheapest route to a controlled environment.


Mixing these up produces the classic failure where a company hires a crew, gets exactly what it asked for, and discovers the brief was wrong. Where full-service creative sits relative to production is covered in our roundup of[full-service creative agencies](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/full-service-creative-agencies) .

### 1. Awesomic


**Best for:** launches where the video and everything around it need to land together.


The reason we open this list is a scheduling one. Most video projects are not slow because filming is slow. They are slow because approval happens after production, when changes are expensive, and because the website, the deck and the social cuts the video points at are commissioned separately and arrive weeks later.


Perseus Defense is the example. The Y Combinator company, building guided micro-missile pods it describes as America's Iron Dome for drones, needed a launch. Our motion expert wrote the script with the founders, then storyboarded the whole video before production so everyone could see exactly what they were approving. Changes happened on the storyboard, where they are free.


The finished launch video was ready in **five days** . It drew more than 500 likes, 20 reposts and 70 comments on LinkedIn, plus another 130 or so interactions on X, totaling over 700 across platforms. In the same engagement we built their brand identity in 10 days and a new website in 11 working days, so the video landed on a site that was ready for it.


That is the trade we offer. We are not a crew with a truck, and for a location shoot with talent and lighting you want one of the companies below. What we do is animation, motion and edited video alongside the brand and web work that surrounds a launch, on one subscription.


**Services:** animated and motion video, scripting and storyboarding, video editing and cutdowns, brand identity, web design and build, decks, social and ad creative.


**Pricing:** the monthly rate is $1,490 for Graphic Pack and $2,995 for All-in-One. A quarterly commitment lowers those to $1,190 and $2,396 across a three-month term. Dedicated Talent, meaning a full-time creative plus a dedicated PM, is scoped directly.


**Proof:** north of 20,000 projects for upwards of 4,000 businesses, 4.9 on Google Play and on Trustpilot, 0.82 percent of applying creatives accepted, a Y Combinator company and a Red Dot holder.


**Our lane:** launches, product video, motion and ongoing edited content. Not principal photography. Teams at scale can see how we structure this on our[mid-market page](https://www.awesomic.com/mid-market) .

### 2. Blue Chalk Media


**Built for:** brands with a real story and the patience to tell it properly.


Blue Chalk Media works from Jay Street in Brooklyn with a second base in Portland, and describes itself as a cinematic nonfiction storytelling agency. The team's roots are in journalism and documentary, and the work shows it.


That background produces a specific kind of film: character-led, reported, and considerably more persuasive than a scripted testimonial when the subject can carry it.


**Services:** documentary-style brand film, interview and profile work, photography, editorial video.


**Pricing:** project-scoped, no public rates.


**Why buyers shortlist it:** documentary craft is difficult to fake, and audiences detect the difference between a real story and a staged one faster than most marketers expect.


### 3. True Film Production


**Built for:** corporate and commercial work that has to happen in more than one city.


True Film Production runs its headquarters on West 30th Street in New York, with additional presence in Charlotte and Miami. That footprint is the practical selling point, since a company shooting in three markets can use one production partner rather than three.


The work spans corporate, commercial and event coverage, which suits organizations with recurring rather than one-off needs.


**Services:** corporate video, commercials, event coverage, animation, post-production.


**Pricing:** quoted per project.


**Its real strength:** multi-city consistency, which is genuinely hard to get from separate local vendors.


### 4. C&I Studios


**Built for:** campaigns that need the idea and the crew from the same place.


C&I Studios lists its international headquarters on East 18th Street in Fort Lauderdale, with offices including Los Angeles, New York, Miami, Atlanta and Washington DC. It positions as a global creative studio rather than a pure production house, covering strategy and creative alongside production.


That breadth suits buyers who do not arrive with a finished concept and would rather not manage an agency and a production company separately.


**Services:** creative and campaign development, video production, post, branding, media.


**Pricing:** scoped per engagement.


**Where it fits:** integrated campaigns where video is the largest component but not the only one.


### 5. Green Buzz Agency


**Built for:** institutions, associations and mission-driven organizations.


Green Buzz Agency names its headquarters as the Washington DC area, on University Drive, and much of its work serves the organizations that cluster there: nonprofits, associations, government contractors and universities.


Those clients bring review processes and compliance constraints that commercial shops often underestimate, and a firm used to them is worth more than a flashier reel.


**Services:** corporate and brand video, documentary, event and conference coverage, animation.


**Pricing:** project-based.


**Why it earns a place here:** the DC institutional market has its own rules, and this is a company that already knows them.


### 6. 100 Sutton Studios


**Built for:** shoots that need a controlled space rather than a location.


100 Sutton Studios operates from Sutton Street in Brooklyn as a production studio with soundstages, which makes it a different proposition from the rest of this list. You are booking space and infrastructure, with production services available on top.


If you have a director and producer already, this is the most cost-efficient path to a controlled shoot in New York.


**Services:** soundstage rental, production support, lighting and grip, studio production.


**Pricing:** stage and equipment rates, quoted by day.


**Where it beats the alternatives:** on any shoot where weather, sound or repeatability would otherwise put the schedule at risk.


### 7. Bonfire Labs


**Built for:** technology brands that need film-grade work at campaign scale.


Bonfire Labs works from Pacific Avenue in San Francisco as a full-service creative studio, sitting close to the technology companies that make up much of its client base. It combines creative development with production and post in one operation.


Proximity to the industry matters here in a way it does not everywhere: a studio that has shot dozens of product launches understands what an unreleased product looks like on camera.


**Services:** creative development, film and video production, motion and animation, post-production.


**Pricing:** enterprise scoping.


**Why buyers shortlist it:** it works at the standard large technology brands expect, without the overhead of a network agency.


### 8. Umault


**Built for:** B2B companies tired of stock-footage handshakes.


Umault operates from Mid America Plaza in Oakbrook Terrace, in the Chicago area, and describes itself as a B2B video ad agency. Its explicit position is that business video does not have to be boring, and its reel backs that up more than most.


B2B is a genuine specialism. The buying committee, the sales cycle and the compliance review are all different from consumer work.


**Services:** B2B video advertising, brand film, campaign creative, video strategy.


**Pricing:** project and campaign scoping.


**Its real strength:** it treats B2B as a creative constraint rather than an excuse, which is rarer in this category than it should be.


### 9. Colormatics


**Built for:** video that has to perform in paid media.


Colormatics works from the Domain in Austin and now presents itself as a full-service ad agency rather than purely a production company, which is worth knowing if you shortlisted it from an older roundup.


That shift tells you what to expect: video made with distribution and performance in mind, including the variant cuts paid social consumes.


**Services:** video production, advertising creative, paid media strategy, content at volume.


**Pricing:** project and retainer.


**Where it fits:** when the video's job is measurable performance rather than brand impression.


### 10. New Revolution Media


**Built for:** Bay Area corporate work with a studio available.


New Revolution Media is based on Missouri Street in San Francisco and covers corporate video, event coverage and branded content, with its own studio space available to rent.


For companies headquartered in the Bay Area, a local crew removes travel costs entirely and makes reshoots practical rather than catastrophic.


**Services:** corporate video, event and conference filming, branded content, studio rental.


**Pricing:** quoted per project, with studio rates separate.


**Why it made this list:** local capacity plus a bookable studio is a genuinely useful combination for recurring corporate needs.


### 11. Studio B Films


**Built for:** brand films made locally but aimed nationally.


Studio B Films describes itself as a local San Francisco Bay Area video production company working on a national scale. That framing is accurate and useful: a regional base with the production standards of a larger market.


The work leans toward brand storytelling rather than straightforward corporate coverage.


**Services:** brand film, commercial production, corporate video, post-production.


**Pricing:** project-based.


**Where it beats the alternatives:** when you want brand-film quality without a Los Angeles cost base attached to it.


### 12. Ball Media Innovations


**Built for:** shoots happening in Florida.


Ball Media Innovations operates across Miami and Orlando and has been producing corporate and commercial video in Florida for a long time. Its site is organized around exactly that: crews, capabilities and coverage in the two markets it serves.


Florida's 1,476 production establishments make it the third-largest state in the industry, and a company with deep local crew relationships is worth more there than a national brand flying people in.


**Services:** corporate video, commercials, testimonial and interview production, event coverage, crew services.


**Pricing:** quoted per project, with crew-only options available.


**Why buyers shortlist it:** if the shoot is in Florida, hiring in Florida removes travel, per diems and a great deal of logistical risk.


## What video production costs in the US


Production quotes vary more than almost any other creative purchase, because the same brief can be executed with two people or twenty. The ranges below reflect the tiers these companies work in.


Type of video Typical range What moves the number


Single-location interview or testimonial $3,000 to $12,000 Crew size, one day or two, edit complexity


Corporate or brand overview film $12,000 to $50,000 Locations, travel, talent, scripting


Documentary-style brand film $30,000 to $120,000 Shoot days, subject availability, edit ratio


National commercial $75,000 to $500,000 Director, talent, licensing, post


Animated or motion video on subscription From $1,490 monthly Volume and how much design sits alongside


Three things move these numbers more than the creative brief does. Shoot days are the biggest, because a crew costs the same whether or not you use the afternoon well. Travel is second, which is the argument for hiring regionally. Talent and music licensing is third, and it is the one buyers forget, since a license limited to twelve months of organic social costs a fraction of a perpetual paid-media license and looks identical on screen.


For comparison, federal wage data puts the 2024 median for producers and directors at $83,480 a year, a role growing 5 percent through 2034 with roughly 12,800 openings annually. Hiring one gets you the person who runs the shoot and none of the equipment, insurance, crew or post pipeline a production company brings, which is why in-house video usually settles at a producer plus external crews rather than a full department.


Scale changes the calculation again at the top end, where the[biggest design agencies](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/biggest-design-agencies) fold production into a much larger retainer and the video line item stops being separable.


## The pre-production questions that control your budget


Almost every overrun is decided before anyone films anything. These are the questions worth settling in writing first:


1. How many shoot days, and what happens to the price if weather or a subject costs you one?
2. Who is on the crew, by role, and is the person in the pitch actually directing?
3. What are the deliverables, including aspect ratios and cutdowns, not just the hero film?
4. What licensing do the music, footage and on-camera talent carry, and for how long?
5. How many edit rounds are included, and what counts as a round?
6. Who owns the raw footage when the project ends?


That last one separates suppliers sharply. Some hand over everything, some archive it and charge for access, and some keep it. None of those is wrong, but discovering the policy two years later when you want to recut is expensive.


Storyboarding belongs in this list too. On the Perseus Defense launch, storyboarding the video before production is what let a five-day turnaround happen at all, because the founders approved a picture of the finished thing rather than a paragraph describing it. The same logic applies to any[AI-assisted production workflow](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/ai-video-production-workflow-a-behind-the-scenes-guide) , where the tools change but the approval bottleneck does not.


## Choosing by what you are actually making


Match the company to the job, in this order.


**A location shoot with talent, lighting and sound** goes to a production company with crew: Blue Chalk, True Film, Green Buzz, New Revolution, Studio B or Ball Media, chosen largely by geography.


**A campaign where the concept is unresolved** goes to a creative agency: C&I Studios, Umault, Colormatics or Bonfire Labs, which will develop the idea before shooting it.


**A controlled studio shoot you are directing yourself** goes to a facility like 100 Sutton Studios, which is the cheapest route when you already have the creative leadership.


**A launch needing video, brand and web together, or ongoing animated and edited content** , is where a subscription makes more sense than per-project quotes, because the second and third video arrive at no extra cost. That comparison against traditional[video production services](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/video-production-services) is mostly a question of volume.


Larger organizations running video across several business units should look at how we handle that on our[enterprise page](https://www.awesomic.com/enterprise) .


## FAQs


### How much does video production cost in the USA?


A single-location interview or testimonial typically runs $3,000 to $12,000, a corporate or brand overview film $12,000 to $50,000, and a documentary-style brand film $30,000 to $120,000. National commercials start around $75,000 and go far higher once you add a name director, talent and broad media licensing. Shoot days, travel and licensing move these numbers more than creative ambition does, which is why a tightly planned two-day shoot often beats a loosely planned one-day shoot on both cost and quality.


### How many video production companies are there in the USA?


Bureau of Labor Statistics figures count 25,298 motion picture and video production establishments in the United States, employing roughly 212,600 people. California has the most at 8,194, followed by New York with 2,874, Florida with 1,476, Texas with 1,251 and Georgia with 940. That scale means your real task is filtering rather than searching, and geography is one of the most practical filters available because it removes travel and per diem costs from the quote.


### Should I hire a local video production company or a national one?


Hire locally unless the work genuinely requires a specialist you cannot find nearby. Travel, accommodation and per diems for a crew add up quickly and buy you nothing on screen, and reshoots become far cheaper when the team is an hour away. States such as Georgia, North Carolina and Florida built deep crew pools through film incentives, so regional capability is stronger than reputation suggests. Reserve national or Los Angeles hires for work where a specific director, a specialist capability or a particular look is the point.


### What is the difference between a video production company and a creative agency?


A production company owns the means of production: crew, cameras, lighting, sound and a post pipeline. Give it a clear brief and it will execute at a high standard. A creative agency starts earlier, developing the concept, script and campaign before producing against it, and charges for that thinking. Choose the agency when what to make is genuinely undecided, and the production company when you know what you want and need it made well. Paying agency rates for a brief you have already written wastes money.


### Who owns the raw footage after a video shoot?


It depends entirely on the contract, and practice varies widely. Some companies hand over all raw footage at the end of the project, some archive it and charge for retrieval, and some retain it as their property. Ask before signing rather than after, particularly if you expect to recut the material for other channels later. The same applies to music, stock footage and on-camera talent, whose licenses normally cap how long, where and in what media the work may run, so a video cleared for organic social may not be cleared for a paid campaign.
